analysis.one_liner: Tightens car and truck exhaust limits and forces cleaner gasoline and diesel, including cuts in carbon dioxide.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in two House subcommittees from October 1989 until the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the Clean Air Act's rules for cars, trucks, buses, and motorcycles: tighter limits on hydrocarbons, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, and soot from new vehicles; longer emissions warranties (10 years or 100,000 miles); onboard computers to catch emission failures; cleaner gasoline (lower summer volatility, oxygen-rich fuel in carbon monoxide areas) and low-sulfur diesel; and a first-of-its-kind mandate to cut carbon dioxide from vehicles 20% by 2005 and 50% by 2025. It was introduced by Rep. David Skaggs with seven cosponsors and referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to two subcommittees where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who breathe air downwind of traffic: tighter tailpipe and fuel standards would cut smog-forming and toxic pollutants, and the carbon dioxide mandate was an early, direct attack on vehicle greenhouse gases [S2][S3]. Residents of high-altitude cities like Denver would benefit from a requirement that cars meet emissions standards at any altitude and from a dedicated high-altitude testing center [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: City residents and people in smoggy or high-altitude areas

how_it_helps.text: Sets specific gram-per-mile limits on hydrocarbons, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, and particulates from new cars, light trucks, heavy trucks, and buses for model years 1991 through 2000 [S2][S3].

Extends the emissions warranty and useful-life period from 5 years/50,000 miles to 10 years/100,000 miles for vehicles made from model year 1995, and bans manufacturers from averaging fleet-wide results to meet a standard [S2][S3].

Requires onboard diagnostic computers, 95%-efficient refueling vapor recovery, best-available evaporative emissions controls, and cold-weather carbon monoxide testing at 20°F — all aimed at pollution that occurs in real driving, not just on the test stand [S2][S3].
Mandates low-sulfur diesel (0.05% by weight), a 10% cap on diesel aromatics, lower-volatility summer gasoline, and oxygenated gasoline in carbon monoxide nonattainment areas each winter [S2][S3].

Requires EPA regulations cutting in-use vehicle carbon dioxide emissions at least 20% by 2005 and 50% by 2025, with a National Academy of Sciences feasibility study — a climate mandate far ahead of anything enacted at the time [S2][S3].
Ends the sale of new vehicles that require leaded gasoline starting model year 1991, and requires all cars to meet standards regardless of sale altitude [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers would bear the cost of redesigning engines, adding onboard diagnostics and vapor recovery, and honoring longer warranties; oil refiners would bear the cost of producing low-sulfur, low-aromatics diesel and reformulated summer gasoline. Those costs would largely be passed to buyers of new vehicles and to drivers at the pump [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Automakers, oil refiners, and new-car buyers

drawbacks.text: Stricter standards and a doubled warranty period would raise the price of new cars, and cleaner fuels would add to pump prices — costs that fall on drivers, including lower-income drivers who buy new vehicles least often and benefit least directly [S3].

The carbon dioxide reduction mandate (20% by 2005, 50% by 2025) was set as a hard requirement before feasibility was known; the bill itself orders a National Academy of Sciences study of whether it is technologically achievable, an unusually backward sequencing for a binding mandate [S3].

The winter oxygenated-fuel mandate (2% then 3.7% oxygen by weight in carbon monoxide areas) would steer gasoline demand toward additives like ethanol and methanol regardless of whether they were the cheapest way to cut carbon monoxide, and the bill even grants oxygenated fuels a one-pound higher volatility allowance [S3].
Small refineries (crude capacity of 175,000 barrels per day or less) would get a five-year exemption from the low-sulfur diesel requirement, giving larger refiners a compliance head start [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case was strong: the bill targeted real-world pollution — cold starts, refueling vapors, high-altitude operation, tampering, and in-use failures — that existing test procedures missed, and its fuel rules were broadly the direction federal law eventually took. The honest cost is that new cars and fuels would have gotten more expensive, and the carbon dioxide mandate was written as a hard number before anyone had shown it was achievable. A well-designed version would have tied the CO2 targets to the feasibility study it commissioned.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 1989, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to two of its subcommittees in October 1989, and never advanced any further before the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Skaggs of Colorado introduced the bill on August 4, 1989, with seven Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S1][S5].
On October 20, 1989, the committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power and the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment — its last recorded action [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action is recorded; the bill died at the end of the 101st Congress on January 3, 1991 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and oil refiners were better off: none of the tighter vehicle standards, longer warranties, onboard diagnostics, or low-sulfur diesel and gasoline requirements took effect from this bill. Drivers avoided any near-term increases in new-car and fuel prices, but city residents kept breathing the pollution the bill would have cut.

for.name: Rep. David Skaggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote its emissions, fuel, and carbon dioxide provisions.

for.name: 7 of 257 House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors (Reps. Schroeder, Owens of Utah, Torres, Panetta, Levine, Edwards, Lantos)

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to two subcommittees and never scheduled a markup or vote on it.

against.name: Rep. John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired never advanced the bill; throughout his tenure he routinely kept vehicle-emissions legislation from reaching the floor without his approval.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors were Democrats and the committee that buried it was run by Democrats, but with no hearings, no votes, and no Republican engagement on the bill itself, the partisan shape cannot be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have forced tighter tailpipe standards, a doubled 10-year/100,000-mile warranty, onboard diagnostics, refueling vapor recovery, and an end to fleet averaging — costly redesigns. Its interest in weaker standards ran against the cleaner air the bill promised the public.

Refiners would have had to produce 0.05% sulfur diesel, cap aromatics at 10%, cut summer gasoline volatility, and blend oxygenated fuel in winter — large capital costs, softened slightly by a small-refinery exemption and a higher volatility allowance for oxygenated fuels.

industries.industry: Ethanol and alternative-fuel producers (methanol, ethanol, natural gas)
industries.note: The oxygenated gasoline mandate and a required minimum share of certified low-emissions vehicles would have created guaranteed demand for ethanol, methanol, and natural gas as motor fuels.
